name: T-Mobile US, Inc.

profile.description: T-Mobile US, Inc. is the second-largest wireless carrier in the United States, serving approximately 125 million customers through its postpaid, prepaid (Metro by T-Mobile), and wholesale brands. Under CEO Srini Gopalan (since November 2025, succeeding Mike Sievert), T-Mobile has transformed from a distant #4 carrier to a #2 powerhouse through the 2020 Sprint merger and continued market share gains. Q2 2026 revenue reached $22.8B (+8% YoY) with industry-leading postpaid service revenue growth of 13% and the highest-ever wireless NPS of 46. The company is expanding into broadband via 5G Home Internet and acquired UScellular's wireless business to strengthen rural coverage. T-Mobile cut 4,500+ jobs in H1 2026 as part of a restructuring to become an AI-enabled, digital-first organization.

innovation.label: STRONG
innovation.analysis: Track Record (3/3): T-Mobile has executed multiple transformative pivots in the last 5 years. The 2020 Sprint merger ($26B+) was the largest wireless deal in U.S. history, creating the nation's second-largest carrier with the largest 5G network. T-Mobile launched 5G Home Internet, disrupting cable broadband incumbents by offering fixed wireless as a competitive alternative. The UScellular wireless acquisition in 2026 extends rural coverage [1][2]. Each move opened significant new revenue streams — Sprint added 50M+ subscribers, 5G Home Internet has become a meaningful growth driver, and UScellular adds rural market access. AI Deployment (1/2): CEO Gopalan has positioned T-Mobile as an 'AI-enabled, data-informed, digital-first' organization, with CTO Dr. John Saw leading integration of AI into network management, customer experience, and cybersecurity [3]. T-Mobile uses AI for customer service optimization and has reported achieving its highest-ever NPS score (46), partly attributed to AI-enhanced experiences. However, no specific AI revenue figures or quantified cost savings have been reported. Market Share (2/2): T-Mobile is the fastest-growing U.S. wireless carrier, adding 277,000 postpaid accounts in Q2 2026 while AT&T and Verizon struggle with flat-to-declining postpaid growth [1]. Postpaid service revenue growth of 13% dramatically outpaces peers. The Un-carrier's share gains have been consistent for 10+ consecutive years, and NPS of 46 is the highest in the industry. Product Pipeline (1/2): T-Mobile's pipeline includes 5G and fixed wireless broadband expansion, AI-enhanced customer experiences, and a 6G technology roadmap under CTO Saw. The UScellular integration provides a near-term growth catalyst with specific integration timelines [3]. However, specific named products with launch dates and revenue visibility beyond the current cycle were not disclosed. R&D Intensity (1/1): T-Mobile invests heavily in network technology, spectrum acquisition, and AI capabilities, with technology spending well above the telecom industry average as the company drives 5G network leadership and AI integration.

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): T-Mobile's 'Un-carrier' identity is a specific, thoughtful purpose that clearly differentiates from AT&T and Verizon — it articulates a vision of challenging industry norms, eliminating pain points, and putting customers first [2]. Created by John Legere and maintained through Mike Sievert and now Srini Gopalan, the Un-carrier positioning has shaped strategic decisions for 10+ years: eliminating contracts, introducing unlimited data, including Netflix, bill transparency. The purpose connects T-Mobile's work to consumer advocacy in a way that goes beyond selling wireless plans. It falls short of a 4 because the cause has not yet been tested through a true existential crisis or multi-decade validation under multiple leadership transitions. Community Impact (1/2): T-Mobile has invested in digital inclusion programs, disaster relief initiatives, and community connectivity. The company committed to net-zero emissions by 2040 and publishes comprehensive corporate responsibility reports. However, no standout foundation or distinctive dollar-amount charitable commitments were identified [5]. Employee Retention (0/2): T-Mobile cut 4,500+ jobs in H1 2026, reducing headcount from 70,036 to 65,365 — a 6.7% workforce reduction [5]. This restructuring environment is inconsistent with strong retention, and the company has gone through three CEO transitions in 5 years (Legere to Sievert to Gopalan), creating leadership instability. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying by executives in the last 12 months was identified.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on available metrics using the growth stock algorithm. T-Mobile's standout metrics are its PEG ratio of 0.78 (well below the 1.0 target, scoring at ceiling with 2x weight), ROE of 17.99% (above the 15% target, at ceiling with 2x weight), and forward P/E of 13.84x (well below the 20 target) [4]. Revenue growth YoY of 9% narrowly misses the 10% target (scoring 0.967), and the 5-year revenue CAGR of ~5% reflects the steady-but-not-explosive post-Sprint integration growth (scoring 0.667 with 2x weight). The primary drags are the elevated D/E ratio of 214% reflecting $120.4B in total debt from the Sprint merger and ongoing network buildout (scoring 0.374), and profit margin of 11.45% — below the 20% target due to the capital-intensive wireless business model (scoring 0.573) [4]. Liquidity is excellent at ~$1B daily trading volume.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): T-Mobile's core wireless business is structurally immune to AI disruption — mobile connectivity requires physical infrastructure (cell towers, spectrum licenses, fiber backhaul) that AI cannot replace or replicate [1]. AI is a net demand driver for wireless carriers: AI applications consume mobile data, AI-powered devices require always-on connectivity, and the proliferation of IoT/AI edge computing increases network utilization. T-Mobile's 5G network is the backbone for AI-enabled services, not a victim of them. The company's fixed wireless broadband expansion (5G Home Internet) faces minimal AI disruption risk as it competes with cable on physical infrastructure. The deduction from 9 reflects that AI could automate customer service operations (T-Mobile's call centers) and potentially reduce the differentiation value of Un-carrier customer experience if AI levels the customer service playing field across carriers [3]. AI Opportunity (0/1): T-Mobile deploys AI extensively in network management, customer experience, and operational optimization, but does not generate separately quantifiable revenue from AI-related products or services sold to customers. AI is a cost optimization and experience enhancement tool, not a revenue line [3].

infinite_game.summary: T-Mobile is a fascinating case for Sinek's framework — the company has demonstrated extraordinary existential flexibility (Sprint merger, broadband entry) and courage to lead (massive capital bets during uncertainty), but its competitive language is often finite ('beating' AT&T and Verizon, 'winning' market share) and its organizational trust has been tested by rapid CEO turnover and significant layoffs. The Un-carrier cause is genuine and has shaped strategic decisions for a decade, but it has not yet been validated through a true existential crisis, and the 4,500+ job cuts in 2026 suggest the cause is subordinate to financial optimization when tested.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): T-Mobile's Un-carrier mission — to disrupt the wireless industry's broken norms and champion consumers through transparent pricing, contract elimination, unlimited data, and superior value — is a genuine cause that has been partially lived for 10+ years [2]. The cause has shaped real strategic decisions: eliminating two-year contracts (2013), introducing unlimited data, including Netflix at no charge, deploying T-Mobile Tuesdays. Multiple CEOs (Legere, Sievert, Gopalan) have maintained the Un-carrier identity, suggesting it transcends individual leadership. However, the cause has not been tested through a genuine existential crisis — the company has been winning in the market for a decade, and the 4,500+ job cuts in 2026 suggest the cause may be subordinate to financial performance when margins are pressured [5].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): T-Mobile's organizational trust is undermined by three factors. First, the company cut 4,500+ jobs in H1 2026, reducing headcount by 6.7% — large-scale layoffs are incompatible with Sinek's Circle of Safety, as employees focus on self-preservation rather than advancing the cause [5]. Second, three CEO transitions in 5 years (Legere to Sievert to Gopalan) creates leadership instability that erodes organizational trust. Third, the restructuring toward an 'AI-enabled, digital-first' organization signals that roles may continue to be automated or eliminated, creating ongoing anxiety about job security [3].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): T-Mobile's competitive language is predominantly finite — the Un-carrier positioning is explicitly defined in opposition to AT&T and Verizon as incumbents to be disrupted and surpassed. Management commentary frequently references 'winning' customers, 'taking share,' and outperforming competitors on NPS and net additions [1][2]. While this competitive fire has driven remarkable growth, Sinek would note that the language is about defeating rivals rather than learning from their strengths. T-Mobile's identity is built on being better THAN the competition rather than better because of the competition.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (2/2): T-Mobile has fundamentally reinvented itself twice. The Sprint merger in 2020 transformed T-Mobile from a distant #4 U.S. carrier struggling to compete with AT&T and Verizon into the #2 carrier with the largest 5G network in the country — a $26B+ bet that required absorbing a failing competitor, integrating redundant networks, and managing massive execution risk [1][2]. The pivot into fixed wireless broadband (5G Home Internet) represents a second reinvention, entering the cable broadband market as a new competitive vector. Both pivots were driven by the Un-carrier cause of challenging industry norms rather than desperation, and both have succeeded, generating meaningful new revenue streams.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (2/2): T-Mobile demonstrates a pattern of costly long-term bets. The Sprint merger ($26B+) required years of regulatory battles, network integration, and billions in capital expenditure during uncertain competitive conditions [1][2]. The company invested aggressively in 5G network buildout when ROI was uncertain, deploying mid-band spectrum at scale before competitors. The UScellular acquisition extends this pattern of courageous capital deployment. CEO Gopalan's decision to restructure toward an AI-enabled organization — cutting 4,500+ jobs — shows willingness to make painful short-term decisions for long-term capability, though Sinek would debate whether this is courage or finite cost optimization [3][5].

investment_thesis: T-Mobile at 13.84x forward earnings with a PEG of 0.78 is the best growth-at-a-reasonable-price opportunity in U.S. telecom — delivering industry-leading 13% postpaid service revenue growth, 12% Core Adjusted EBITDA growth to $9.5B quarterly, and EPS of $2.99 that beat consensus by $0.41 [1][4]. The company's structural advantages — largest 5G network, superior spectrum holdings, and highest wireless NPS (46) — are widening the competitive gap against AT&T and Verizon, translating to consistent postpaid account net additions (277K in Q2 2026) while peers struggle. T-Mobile's free cash flow of $18.4B annually funds a $4.08/share dividend (2.36% yield), aggressive share buybacks, and strategic acquisitions (UScellular). The fixed wireless broadband opportunity adds a second growth vector as T-Mobile leverages 5G to disrupt cable incumbents in underserved markets.
thesis_continued: The bear case centers on leverage, competitive sustainability, and execution risk from leadership transitions. T-Mobile carries $120.4B in debt (D/E 214%), a legacy of the Sprint merger that limits financial flexibility and creates refinancing risk in a higher-rate environment [4]. The 5-year revenue CAGR of only 5% reflects that organic growth ex-Sprint has been modest, and the current 9% YoY growth rate may decelerate as the UScellular integration dilutes near-term margins. The Un-carrier competitive advantage may be narrowing — AT&T and Verizon are improving their networks, matching T-Mobile's value positioning, and deploying their own AI capabilities. Three CEO transitions in 5 years (Legere to Sievert to Gopalan) create strategic continuity risk, and the 4,500+ job cuts in H1 2026 signal that T-Mobile is shifting from growth-at-all-costs to efficiency optimization — a potentially finite game shift [3][5]. The Inspire Impact Score of -67 (MISALIGNED) limits allocation for faith-based investors. A widespread network outage in 2026 that affected 140,000+ users highlights operational reliability concerns that could increase regulatory scrutiny and customer churn.
key_catalysts: UScellular wireless acquisition integration providing rural market expansion and approximately 4.5 million new subscribers, extending T-Mobile's network coverage advantage and adding a new revenue growth vector in underserved markets [2]

Fixed wireless broadband (5G Home Internet) scaling as T-Mobile's superior mid-band 5G spectrum enables competitive speeds in cable markets — broadband revenue is growing double-digits and represents T-Mobile's disruption of the $100B+ cable broadband market [1]

AI-enabled operational transformation under CTO John Saw driving cost efficiencies and customer experience improvements — the highest-ever NPS of 46 demonstrates network quality and service differentiation are widening competitive moats [1][3]
key_risks: Debt burden of $120.4B (D/E 214%) from Sprint merger creates refinancing risk in higher-rate environments and limits financial flexibility — any significant interest rate increase could compress free cash flow available for dividends and buybacks [4]

CEO succession instability — three CEO transitions in 5 years (Legere to Sievert to Gopalan) risks strategic discontinuity, and new CEO Gopalan's digital-first, AI-enabled vision represents a cultural shift that may face execution challenges or organizational resistance [3]

Network reliability risk highlighted by a widespread 2026 outage affecting 140,000+ users and disrupting MVNO partners (Mint Mobile, Boost Mobile), potentially increasing regulatory scrutiny and eroding customer trust built by the Un-carrier brand [3]
